items.title: What an APPROVER can see in the run list
items.body:
`buildRunVisibilityWhere` asks `canReadAllRuns(user.role)`, which is simply `role !== "VIEWER"`. For an APPROVER that is true, so the where clause is empty and every run is visible. Only a VIEWER gets `{ startedById: user.id }`. The review marks this as an "info" finding: confirm it is intended.

- Runs awaiting that approver is a sensible design, but no such filter exists.
- Own runs only is the VIEWER rule, not the APPROVER one.
- No runs is wrong: the APPROVER role includes `runs:read` in the permission matrix.

excerpts.quote: export function buildRunVisibilityWhere(user: Pick<User, "id" | "role">): Prisma.WorkflowRunWhereInput { if (canReadAllRuns(user.role)) { return {}; } // ⚠️ SENIOR NOTE: VIEWER users only see runs they started; dropping this filter is a direct data leak. return { startedById: user.id }; }
export function canReadAllRuns(role: UserRole) { return role !== "VIEWER"; }

items.title: Why PENDING cannot jump straight to SUCCEEDED
items.body:
The run state machine is a lookup table. `runTransitions.PENDING` is `["RUNNING", "CANCELLED"]`, so "SUCCEEDED" is not allowed and `assertValidRunTransition` throws `Invalid run transition from PENDING to SUCCEEDED.` A run has to start running before it can succeed.

- Any status reaching SUCCEEDED is wrong: SUCCEEDED, FAILED and CANCELLED are terminal and only RUNNING leads to SUCCEEDED.
- Remaining steps play no part: the function only looks at the two statuses.
- Returning false is wrong: the function has no return value; it throws.

excerpts.quote: const runTransitions: Record<RunStatus, RunStatus[]> = { PENDING: ["RUNNING", "CANCELLED"], RUNNING: ["WAITING_APPROVAL", "SUCCEEDED", "FAILED", "CANCELLED"], WAITING_APPROVAL: ["RUNNING", "FAILED", "CANCELLED"], SUCCEEDED: [], FAILED: [], CANCELLED: [], };
export function assertValidRunTransition(from: RunStatus, to: RunStatus) { if (!runTransitions[from].includes(to)) { throw new Error(`Invalid run transition from ${from} to ${to}.`); } }

items.title: Idempotency keys: what the server remembers about a retry
items.body:
Clients retry. A network blip, a double click or a timeout can send the same "start this run" request twice. An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry: the client sends a key, the server remembers which run that key produced, and a repeat is answered from that memory instead of creating new work.

Two design questions decide how such a scheme behaves. First, whose key is it? Look at line 51 of `workflow-run-service.ts` and write down exactly what string is stored as the key. Second, what counts as "the same request"? Read the replay branch and note which fields of the new request it compares, if any, before it returns.

Also look at how the lookup and the insert relate: are they one statement or two, and what does the catch block do?

items.title: Creating and seeding a run: count the transactions
items.body:
Starting a run writes several rows: the run itself, its first event and its first executable step. `startWorkflowRun` creates the run, and a separate function, `seedRunExecution` in `workflow-engine-service.ts`, writes the first event and step.

The course asks you to reason about how those writes are grouped into transactions, what a failure part-way through would leave behind, and how later requests (a replay of the same key, the worker) would treat that state. The service carries a comment about this, and the permission model has a related permission: check whether any route or service actually uses it.

While reading, list every database write in order, mark which `$transaction` call it belongs to, and note where each transaction ends.

items.title: Why an in-flight run keeps its starting version
items.body:
When the run is created, the service writes `workflowVersionId: activeVersion.id` and `currentStepKey: definition.initialStepKey`, both taken from the version that was active at that moment. Nothing later rewrites those fields when another version is activated, so the run keeps following v1.

- Following the active version would change a run's steps halfway through, which is exactly what freezing prevents.
- Splitting by step is wrong: there is a single `workflowVersionId` per run.
- Cancelling runs on activation is wrong: no code path does that.

excerpts.quote: return createWorkflowRun(tx, { workflowVersionId: activeVersion.id, startedById: user.id, displayName: input.displayName, idempotencyKey: scopedIdempotencyKey, input: input.input as Prisma.InputJsonValue, context: input.input as Prisma.InputJsonValue, status: "PENDING", currentStepKey: definition.initialStepKey, });

The run stores `workflowVersionId: activeVersion.id` (line 68). Activating a newer version later does not change in-flight runs. The `currentStepKey` comes from the parsed definition of **that** version (line 75).

items.title: Why a replay with a new payload returns the old run
items.body:
The first thing `startWorkflowRun` does is build the scoped key `u1:k` and look it up. A run exists, so `if (existing) return existing;` fires. The new displayName and input are never read. The concepts chapter calls this deliberate request identity, not payload equality.

- Updating the original run is wrong: the replay branch performs no write at all.
- A 409 would need a stored request fingerprint to compare against, which this service does not keep (the review lists that as finding 3).
- A second run is wrong for the same reason: nothing hashes the payload, so the key alone decides.

excerpts.quote: const scopedIdempotencyKey = `${user.id}:${input.idempotencyKey}`; const existing = await findWorkflowRunByIdempotencyKey(scopedIdempotencyKey); if (existing) { return existing; }
- One user replaying `k` gets the original run back, even with a different `displayName` or `input` (test line 26).

items.title: The fix for the losing concurrent create
items.body:
The worked exercise wraps the creation transaction in `try/catch`. In the catch it tests for Prisma's unique-violation code `P2002`, re-runs `findWorkflowRunByIdempotencyKey(scopedIdempotencyKey)` and returns the run the winner created. A lab case then makes the create double throw P2002 after inserting a row and asserts that the result is that row and that seeding is not called again.

- Retrying with a fresh key would create a second run and break idempotency.
- P2025 is Prisma's "record not found" code, not a unique violation.
- Returning 409 is still an error for the client, when the point is to behave like a replay.

excerpts.quote: **Goal:** Change `startWorkflowRun` so that a unique-key collision returns the winner's run instead of a 500. **Check:** (1) Wrap the `$transaction` (66-77) in `try/catch`. (2) In the catch, test for Prisma's unique-violation code `P2002`. (3) Re-run `findWorkflowRunByIdempotencyKey(scopedIdempotencyKey)` and return its result. (4) Add a lab case whose `createWorkflowRun` double throws `Object.assign(new Error('dup'), { code: 'P2002' })` after inserting a row under that key. Assert that the result is that row and that no `seed` call happens. (5) State in the PR that a real-database race test is still needed.

items.title: Why the same key from two users makes two runs
items.body:
The service never stores the raw client key. It stores `${user.id}:${input.idempotencyKey}`. For u1 that is `u1:k` and for u2 it is `u2:k`, so u2's lookup finds nothing and a new run is created. The lab asserts that u2 gets a new id and that the map of runs grows to two.

- Returning u1's run would leak another user's run; the user-scoped key prevents it.
- A 409 is wrong: there is no conflict, the keys are different strings.
- Refusing a shared key is wrong: clients may pick any key; scoping makes them independent.

excerpts.quote: const scopedIdempotencyKey = `${user.id}:${input.idempotencyKey}`;
4. `u2` gets a new id, the key `u2:k`, and `runs.size` becomes 2.

items.title: Start here: one function, startWorkflowRun
items.body:
ww19 is a workflow-orchestration app built on Next.js route handlers, Prisma and PostgreSQL. The whole `astraupskill/` course follows a single function: `startWorkflowRun` in `src/services/workflow-run-service.ts`. It is about fifty lines long, so open it and keep it beside every chapter.

Read the README first: it lists the seven steps of the function in order. Then `02-CONCEPTS.md` explains the ideas, `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` walks through the five lab cases call by call, and `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md` ends with a senior review table of findings across the repo.

A good habit for this quest: before each quiz, say which line of `startWorkflowRun` the question is really about. Most answers follow from where a `return` or a `throw` sits.

excerpts.quote: ww19 is a workflow-orchestration app. It is built on Next.js route handlers with Prisma and PostgreSQL (`prisma/migrations/202604121613_init/migration.sql`), and it uses real database-backed sessions (`src/lib/auth/session.ts`), versioned workflow definitions, a step engine, approvals, and a separate worker process (`src/worker/index.ts`). This course follows one entry point: `startWorkflowRun` in [`src/services/workflow-run-service.ts`](../src/services/workflow-run-service.ts), lines 42-92.

The wider set of concepts this repo demonstrates.

items.title: Why a replay ignores a retired definition
items.body:
The replay check is the very first step, and it returns before the version lookup and the definition parse. So when the same user sends the same key again, the service never asks whether the definition still has an active version. It just returns the stored run. The concepts chapter calls this correct for idempotency, with the side effect that retiring a definition does not affect replays. The review notes that no test covers it.

- A 404 would need the version lookup, which the replay skips.
- A parse failure would need the parse, which is also skipped.
- A new run on another version is wrong: replays never create anything.

excerpts.quote: const existing = await findWorkflowRunByIdempotencyKey(scopedIdempotencyKey); if (existing) { return existing; } const activeVersion = await findActiveWorkflowVersionForDefinition(input.workflowDefinitionId);

The version lookup and the definition parse both run before the transaction. A missing active version gives 404 with no writes, and a parse failure writes nothing (test lines 29-34). Because the replay branch returns before both, a replay **skips** validation entirely. That is correct for idempotency, but it means a definition retired after the first call does not affect replays.

items.title: What a seed failure leaves behind
items.body:
The run is created inside `db.$transaction` and that transaction finishes before `seedRunExecution` is called. Seeding opens its own `$transaction` to append the RUN_CREATED event and create the first executable step. If seeding throws, only its own transaction rolls back. The run row is already committed, still PENDING, with no event and no step, so nothing can advance it.

- Rolling the run back is what a single shared transaction would do; this code uses two.
- A FAILED run is wrong: nothing updates the run's status after the error, and the event was never written.
- A queued first step is wrong: creating that step was part of the rolled-back seed transaction.

excerpts.quote: const workflowRun = await db.$transaction(async (tx) => { return createWorkflowRun(tx, { workflowVersionId: activeVersion.id, startedById: user.id, displayName: input.displayName, idempotencyKey: scopedIdempotencyKey, input: input.input as Prisma.InputJsonValue, context: input.input as Prisma.InputJsonValue, status: "PENDING", currentStepKey: definition.initialStepKey, }); }); // ⚠️ SENIOR NOTE: The run is created before execution starts so a crash between creation and first-step scheduling still leaves a durable record to repair. await seedRunExecution({ workflowRun, definition, });

}) { return db.$transaction(async (tx) => { await appendExecutionEvent(tx, { workflowRunId: params.workflowRun.id, actorType: "USER", actorUserId: params.workflowRun.startedById, eventType: "RUN_CREATED", toStatus: params.workflowRun.status, message: "Workflow run created.", payload: { currentStepKey: params.definition.initialStepKey, }, }); return createNextExecutableStep(tx, params.workflowRun, params.definition, params.definition.initialStepKey); });

items.title: Why a replay still answers 201 Created
items.body:
The POST handler calls `startWorkflowRun(user, body)` and then always returns `jsonOk(run, { status: 201 })`. The service returns a run in both cases, new or replayed, and gives the route no flag to tell them apart, so the status is the same. The senior review lists this as a low-severity finding because clients cannot tell a replay from a fresh create.

- 200 OK would need the route to know it was a replay, which it does not.
- 409 is wrong: a replay is a successful outcome here.
- 303 See Other is a reasonable design elsewhere, but nothing in this route redirects.

excerpts.quote: export async function POST(request: NextRequest) { try { const user = await requireRequestUser(request, permissions.runsStart); const body = startWorkflowRunSchema.parse(await request.json()); const run = await startWorkflowRun(user, body); return jsonOk(run, { status: 201 });

items.title: Why a missing active version fails before any write
items.body:
After the replay check misses, the service calls `findActiveWorkflowVersionForDefinition`. With no active version it gets null and throws `ApiError(404, ...)`. That happens before `workflowDefinitionSchema.parse` and before the transaction, so the lab sees only the `lookup` and `version` calls and no rows.

- A 500 from parsing is wrong: the parse is never reached.
- Creating a run is wrong: validation happens before any side effect, which is the point of chapter 02 section 4.
- A 400 from Zod is wrong: this is a lookup result, not body validation, and the service throws an explicit 404.

excerpts.quote: const activeVersion = await findActiveWorkflowVersionForDefinition(input.workflowDefinitionId); if (!activeVersion) { throw new ApiError(404, "No active workflow version found for this definition."); } const definition = workflowDefinitionSchema.parse(activeVersion.definition);
## Case 2: missing version (29-31) 404 (`e.status === 404`, the real `ApiError`). Calls: `lookup, version`. No rows.

items.title: Why the losing concurrent request gets a 500
items.body:
The lookup and the insert are separate statements, so two simultaneous first requests can both see "no run" and both call `createWorkflowRun`. The `idempotencyKey` column on `WorkflowRun` is `@unique`, so the database accepts one insert and rejects the other with a Prisma unique-constraint error. `jsonError` only recognises `ApiError`; anything else is logged and returned as a 500.

- Merging is not something a database does; one insert simply fails.
- Two runs under one key is impossible because of the unique index.
- A 409 replay is the fix the worked exercise proposes, not current behaviour.

excerpts.quote: idempotencyKey String? @unique
console.error(error); return NextResponse.json( { error: { message: "Internal server error.", details: null } }, { status: 500 }, );

items.title: Why a malformed body becomes a 500
items.body:
The route parses the body with `startWorkflowRunSchema.parse`, which throws a `ZodError` when `idempotencyKey` is missing. The catch hands it to `jsonError`. That function only special-cases `ApiError`; every other error is logged and answered with a 500 "Internal server error." and `details: null`. The review lists this as a low finding: a bad request should be a 400.

- A 400 with issues is the desirable behaviour, but there is no `ZodError` branch to produce it.
- 422 is likewise never emitted.
- A generated key is wrong: the route does not fill in missing fields.

excerpts.quote: export function jsonError(error: unknown) { if (error instanceof ApiError) { return NextResponse.json( { error: { message: error.message, details: error.details ?? null } }, { status: error.status }, ); } console.error(error); return NextResponse.json( { error: { message: "Internal server error.", details: null } }, { status: 500 }, );
const body = startWorkflowRunSchema.parse(await request.json());
